content.title: Lever as an applicant tracking system
content.body: Our records give Lever the tagline "Applicant tracking system and recruiting platform," and the rest of the repository treats it consistently as an ATS rather than an HR suite. Our HR technology guide uses it as its example of what a company should graduate to once it hires more than twenty people a year, and our recruiting pricing guide lists the functions this class performs: job postings, resume collection, candidate communication, interview scheduling, and offer management. Nothing in our files places payroll, benefits, or the employee record inside Lever; those stay in the system it hands off to.

content.title: Interview kits, scorecards, and pipeline reporting
content.body: Our HR technology guide groups Lever with dedicated platforms that carry structured interview kits, scorecard-based candidate evaluation, and reporting on source quality and time-to-hire. Its threshold matters for fit: this class is recommended once a company hires more than twenty people a year, and the guide names Lever again at seventy-five to two hundred employees when recruiting volume justifies the upgrade. Set against the pricing guide's list of ATS functions, the picture is a tool organized around the requisition — from the posting through the interview loop to the offer — with reporting showing where candidates came from and how long each stage took.

content.title: Where our comparisons land on Lever
content.body: Eight comparison files pair Lever with another HR product, and the recorded outcomes are consistent enough to list in full: three of the eight go Lever's way, five to the opponent, and in every case the deciding row is the user rating — no capability row separates these products in our files. The set is recorded as follows:
items: A win over ADP, where the recorded rating of 4.2 beats 4 and the price row is marked for both sides
A win over Workday at 4.2 against its recorded 4.1, one of the two pairings where Lever holds the higher rating
A win over Zoho People in the one pairing where both products are recorded at 4.2
Losses to BambooHR, Greenhouse, Gusto, HiBob, and Rippling, each decided by the opponent's higher recorded rating
A starting price recorded on both sides of each of the eight pairings, so no verdict here rests on price
A rating of 4.2 out of 5 from 540 reviews that every comparison and alternatives line agrees with

content.title: The band on this page against the models our guide describes
content.body: This page records Lever at $80-120/mo, and seven of its eight comparison descriptions carry that band in full. The wider market picture in our files is less tidy: our recruiting pricing guide describes applicant tracking systems priced per employee per month, per active job posting, or on custom enterprise contracts bundling implementation and support, and it states that none of the platforms it evaluates carry published pricing verification. Our HR category page goes a third way, pricing recruiting-specific tools on annual contracts. Three models across three of our own pages, no agreed unit — confirm exact rates with the vendor before budgeting.

content.title: The applicant-to-HRIS handoff
content.body: The integration our HR technology guide calls the key point in this stack is the handoff from applicant tracking to HRIS: when a candidate accepts an offer, the employee record, IT provisioning, payroll setup, and benefits enrollment have to begin in the next system without a manual relay. Our employee onboarding glossary describes that mechanism in detail, naming Greenhouse as its example but speaking of applicant tracking systems as a class — a class our records place Lever in. The practical reading for buyers is that Lever's value at this boundary depends on what the receiving HRIS supports, a detail no page in our repository records for Lever specifically.

content.title: What Lever is not recorded as doing
content.body: The limits our files place on Lever are mostly structural. It is an applicant tracking system, so payroll, benefits administration, and the employee record sit outside its recorded scope by construction. It is recorded as a paid product, with no free tier named anywhere in our dataset. Published pricing verification is absent — our pricing guide says so for every platform it covers. Beyond recruiting, our files describe no module for Lever: no performance management, no learning content, no core HR. With no certifications recorded either, a security review has nothing in this repository to draw on.

content.title: Delivery, support, and certifications on file
content.body: Our dataset records Lever as delivered from the cloud with an API field marked available, which is the structural part of its delivery picture. Beyond that the record thins out fast: no vendor certification for Lever appears anywhere in this repository, no support tiers are described, and no data residency or uptime commitments are on file. The comparison pages carry ease-of-use and integration-ecosystem rows, but both sides are marked in every pairing, so those rows assert nothing specific about Lever as a product. Anything in this area should be checked against the vendor's current documentation rather than inferred from these pages.

content.title: How the rankings place Lever
content.body: Lever's ranking footprint is unusual in this cluster. It sits at number four in our recruiting software ranking and appears at a consistent position across the segment pages for agencies, enterprise teams, freelancers, remote teams, small businesses, and startups, each labeled with a best-for line about scaling. It is also seventh in our HR platforms list. The distinguishing placement is in the small-team answers: Lever is the only product named in both the recruiting software answer (with Greenhouse and BambooHR) and the HR platforms answer (with Workday and ADP), making it the common recommendation across two of our rankings for smaller teams.

content.title: What these statements are built from
content.body: The statements here were distilled from this repository's stored files on Lever — its review fields, the ranking pages that carry it, the eight comparison files, the HR guides, and the alternatives pages — instead of any account of using it. The 4.2 rating and 540-review count are the values stored on this page, and they agree with every other file that quotes them. Where our pages disagree — on the unit of its pricing, on published verification — both readings are reported above rather than settled in favor of one.

faqs.question: What kind of product is Lever, on this record?
faqs.answer: Our tagline files it as an applicant tracking system and recruiting platform. Payroll, benefits, and the employee record sit outside that scope, in the HRIS a candidate is handed off to.

faqs.question: What does Lever cost, and can that figure be trusted?
faqs.answer: This page records a band of $80-120/mo, carried in seven of its eight comparison descriptions. Our pricing guide says none of the platforms it evaluates have published pricing verification, so confirm exact rates with the vendor.

faqs.question: How does Lever fare against Greenhouse and Workday?
faqs.answer: It loses the Greenhouse pairing, recorded at 4.3 against Lever's 4.2, and wins the Workday pairing at 4.2 against 4.1. Across all eight pairings the recorded split is three wins and five losses.

faqs.question: Where does Lever sit in our rankings?
faqs.answer: Number four in our recruiting software ranking and seventh in our HR platforms list, with a consistent position on the segment pages. It is the only product our small-team answers name in both recruiting and HR platforms.

faqs.question: Does Lever handle the handoff to an HRIS?
faqs.answer: Our HR technology guide calls that handoff the key integration point for this class of tool, and our onboarding glossary describes the mechanism — offer acceptance starting onboarding in the receiving system — for applicant trackers generally.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Centered on configuring the pipeline and interview kits; our files carry no rollout or training data either way
whoShouldUse: Companies hiring more than twenty people a year that need a dedicated applicant tracking layer, and smaller teams our two ranking answers name Lever as a starting point for recruiting and HR platforms.
whoShouldNotUse: Buyers who need payroll, benefits, or employee records in the same system, and anyone budgeting from this page alone — our pricing guide says published pricing verification is absent.
